title: Thermal interface materials for extreme heat flux
bottleneck: Heat must cross from silicon to heat spreaders through thermal interface materials (TIMs), but current TIMs (0.1-0.5 K·cm2/W) can't handle the 500 W/cm2 hotspots of advanced chiplet packages. Materials that are thermally excellent (solders, liquid metals) suffer pump-out, corrosion, or mechanical stress under thermal cycling, while compliant polymers insulate too well. No TIM simultaneously delivers high conductivity, compliance, and decades-long reliability.
why_it_blocks: The TIM is the narrowest thermal choke point in the package; its resistance directly sets junction temperatures and throttling points. Without better TIMs, chiplet roadmaps must either underclock or adopt exotic cooling, both of which raise total cost of ownership.
current_state: Liquid-metal, sintered-silver, and carbon-based TIMs show lab performance well above conventional greases, and some ship in high-end products. Long-term reliability data under server thermal cycling is still thin.
